title: Kɔkɔɔbɔ sɛnkyerɛnee / Negotiating and Persuading
bridge: In Twi, negotiating and persuading often involve indirect expressions and proverbs to maintain harmony, unlike English where directness is more common. Be cautious with literal translations, as Twi relies heavily on context and cultural nuances. Avoid being overly assertive, as it may be perceived as rude. Instead, use polite phrases and proverbs to build consensus.
rule: When negotiating or persuading in Twi, use modal verbs like 'sɛ' (if) and 'pɛ' (want) to express desires or conditions. Proverbs (mmatapa) are frequently used to strengthen arguments subtly. Always start with respectful phrases like 'Mepɛ sɛ...' (I would like...) or 'Sɛ yɛbɛyɛ...' (If we do...). Avoid direct refusals; instead, use phrases like 'Ɛyɛ dɔ' (It's difficult) or 'Mennim' (I don't know) to soften the response.

title: Ma akwantufoɔ ne ma ayɛ adwene / Giving and justifying opinions
bridge: In Twi, expressing and justifying opinions involves a more communal and contextual approach compared to English. While English often emphasizes individual perspectives, Twi tends to incorporate collective wisdom and proverbs to support arguments. Be cautious of directly translating English idioms, as Twi relies heavily on figurative language and cultural references. Additionally, Twi uses specific verb constructions to express certainty or doubt, which may not align directly with English equivalents.
rule: To give and justify opinions in Twi, use the structure 'Mɛma akwantufoɔ' (I give my opinion) followed by 'Efisɛ...' (Because...) to provide justification. For deeper explanations, incorporate proverbs or cultural references using 'Sɛ... na' (As... says). When expressing certainty, use 'Mɛhu' (I believe) or 'Mɛbɔ dɔɔ' (I strongly believe). For doubt, use 'Mɛdɔ' (I doubt) or 'Mɛntumi abɔ dɔɔ' (I cannot strongly agree). Remember that Twi values indirectness, so avoid overly assertive language.

concept_examples.translation: I give my opinion that this country is good or bad because if someone doesn’t take care of themselves, no one will.

title: Especular sobre el pasado / Hypothesising about the past
bridge: In Twi, hypothesising about the past often involves the use of conditional structures and specific verb forms, similar to English. However, Twi relies more on context and verb conjugations rather than auxiliary verbs like 'would' or 'could'. English speakers might over-rely on direct translations, leading to errors in tense and modality. Additionally, Twi uses the verb 'sɛ' (to be) in conditional sentences, which doesn't always have a direct equivalent in English.
rule: To hypothesise about the past in Twi, use the conditional form of the verb, often preceded by 'sɛ' (if). The structure is: 'Sɛ + subject + verb (conditional form) + object'. For example, 'Sɛ me kɔe, me bɛka' (If I had gone, I would have bought). Note that the conditional form of the verb is typically the same as the future tense form in Twi. Exceptions include irregular verbs, which must be memorized. This structure is used to speculate about past events that did not occur or had different outcomes.

Twi requires both clauses to use the conditional form or past tense for hypothesising about the past. The correct structure is 'Sɛ + subject + past tense verb + object, subject + conditional verb + object.'

title: Kasa nkyerɛkyerɛ nnɔm / Discussing Abstract Concepts
bridge: In Twi, discussing abstract concepts often involves idiomatic expressions and proverbs, which can be more direct and figurative than in English. English speakers might struggle with the literal translation of Twi idioms, leading to misunderstandings. Additionally, Twi uses a subject-object-verb (SOV) sentence structure for complex ideas, whereas English typically follows a subject-verb-object (SVO) pattern. Be cautious of false cognates and the contextual use of abstract nouns.
rule: When discussing abstract concepts in Twi, use proverbs (mmatapa) and idiomatic expressions to convey deeper meanings. Abstract nouns often require specific contextual verbs like 'kɔ’ (to be) or 'yɛ’ (to exist). For example, 'honesty' (ntɔfrɛ) is often expressed as 'ɔkɔ yɛ ntɔfrɛ' (it is honesty). Avoid direct translations of English phrases, as Twi relies heavily on figurative language. Use the SOV structure for complex sentences, e.g., 'Onyame a ɔdɔɔ so ara na ɔde ma no ho adwuma' (God, because He loves Himself, works on His own).

title: Kyerεw Kronkron / Expressing Nuanced Emotions
bridge: In Twi, expressing complex emotions often involves idiomatic expressions and proverbs, unlike English where direct statements are more common. Twi speakers frequently use figurative language to convey subtle emotional shades, which can be challenging for English speakers who may over-rely on literal translations. Be cautious of false cognates like 'ani gua' (I'm tired), which doesn't always mean physical fatigue but can express emotional exhaustion.
rule: To express nuanced emotions in Twi, combine emotional verbs with intensifiers or contextual adverbs. For example, 'Mεyε me ho adwuma' (I'm overwhelmed) uses 'adwuma' (work) metaphorically to convey emotional burden. Proverbs like 'εbεyε dεn a εbεyε dεn' (it will end in tears) are often used to express foreboding or sadness. Note that tone and context are crucial, as the same phrase can convey different emotions depending on delivery.

title: Nkitahodi ne Mmɛda: Formal Writing in Twi / Formal Writing: Reports and Emails
bridge: In Twi, formal writing, especially in reports and emails, requires a more structured and respectful tone compared to English. While English uses titles like 'Mr.' or 'Ms.', Twi often incorporates honorifics directly into sentences. Additionally, Twi sentences tend to be more concise, with a focus on clarity and directness, which can feel less wordy than English. Be cautious of overusing English-style politeness phrases, as Twi has its own subtle ways of conveying respect.
rule: In formal Twi writing, use the appropriate honorifics such as 'Nana' (for chiefs), 'Opanin/Opanyin' (for elderly men/women), or 'Mr./Mrs.' equivalents like 'Okyeame' (for secretaries or spokespersons). Sentences should be clear and direct, avoiding unnecessary phrases. Use the standard Twi sentence structure (Subject-Verb-Object) and ensure proper noun agreement. For reports, use the past tense to describe completed actions and the future tense for planned activities. In emails, start with a respectful greeting like 'Mepa wo hyia' (I greet you) and end with 'Medaase' (Thank you).

title: Kɔkɔdɔm na Mmɛbɛsa / Managing Conflicts and Misunderstandings
bridge: In Twi, addressing conflicts requires a nuanced approach compared to English. While English often emphasizes directness, Twi prioritizes politeness and indirectness to maintain harmony. For instance, Twi uses proverbs or indirect phrases to soften criticism, whereas English might use straightforward statements. Be cautious not to translate English phrases like 'You’re wrong' directly, as this can come across as overly harsh in Twi.
rule: When dealing with conflict in Twi, use indirect expressions and proverbs to convey your point without causing offense. The verb 'kɔkɔ' (to quarrel) is rarely used directly; instead, phrases like 'ɛyɛ dɛn' (it’s like this) or 'sɛ woyɛ' (if you do) are preferred to introduce disagreements. Proverbs such as 'Aboɔ ne apue' (The mouth and the stomach) are often used to diplomatically address issues. Always maintain a respectful tone, even when expressing disagreement.

title: Kɔso ne Asoɔmerɛ / Summarising and Paraphrasing
bridge: In Twi, summarising and paraphrasing often involve more contextual and situational cues than in English. While English relies heavily on specific verbs and phrases like 'in other words' or 'to sum up,' Twi uses proverbs, idioms, and indirect expressions to convey the same meaning. Be cautious of over-literal translations, as Twi summaries may omit details assumed to be common knowledge. Additionally, Twi paraphrasing often includes cultural references that may not directly translate to English.
rule: To summarise in Twi, use phrases like 'N'asɛm a ɛyɛ ne...' (The point is...) or 'Wɔbɛka sɛ...' (It can be said that...). For paraphrasing, rephrase ideas using synonyms or proverbs, such as 'Sɛ woka a, woyɛ...' (If you say it, it means...). Avoid direct repetition and instead focus on capturing the essence of the original statement. Proverbs like 'Apaa wasan ntoma' (The parrot does not weave a cloth) can be used to rephrase ideas indirectly. Ensure the paraphrase maintains the original meaning while adapting to the cultural context.

title: Nkwa abuasɛm / Using Idioms Naturally
bridge: In Twi, idioms (abuasm) are often more literal and tied to cultural references than in English. For example, the Twi idiom 'Ɛda a ɛkye yie' (The mouth that speaks the truth) doesn't have a direct English equivalent like 'speak the truth.' Be cautious of translating English idioms directly, as they may not exist in Twi or have different meanings. Focus on learning Twi idioms in context to avoid misunderstandings.
rule: Twi idioms are fixed expressions that often cannot be understood from their individual words. They are used to convey specific meanings or emotions. Common idioms are tied to proverbs, nature, or everyday life. Learn them as whole phrases and practice using them in appropriate situations. Note that some idioms may have regional variations or be more common in spoken than written Twi.

title: Kyerεw Kronkron ne Akwanmu / Academic and Professional Register
bridge: In Twi, the academic and professional register is more formal and structured than in English. While English uses titles like 'Dr.' or 'Prof.', Twi employs specific honorifics and verb forms to convey respect. Beware of directly translating English phrases like 'in my opinion' or 'regarding this matter,' as Twi uses distinct expressions that emphasize humility and clarity. Additionally, Twi often omits subjects when they are clear from context, unlike English, which can lead to overly wordy sentences if not adapted.
rule: In Twi, the academic and professional register relies on honorifics (e.g., 'Nana' for elders, 'Opanin' for respected men) and formal verb forms (e.g., 'de ma wo akwaaba' instead of 'εyɛ akwaaba'). Indirect expressions are preferred for opinions (e.g., 'Sε me nteaseε,...' instead of 'Mεduru so...'). Avoid contractions and colloquialisms. Sentence structure is often subject-verb-object, but subjects can be omitted if contextually clear. Use precise vocabulary and avoid literal translations of English phrases.
